result.summary: At a Bacchic festival Progne, disguised as a reveler, rescues her mute sister Philomela from captivity. Together they kill Progne's son Itys and serve him to Tereus at a feast, then reveal the truth. Tereus pursues them with a sword and all three are changed into birds.

scenes.title: Progne rescues Philomela
scenes.summary: Dressed as a Bacchante, Progne breaks into the lonely dwelling, seizes Philomela, disguises her in Bacchic garb and leads her into the palace, where she unveils her.
scenes.stakes: Discovery by Tereus would doom both sisters; Philomela is shamed and terrified.

scenes.title: The murder of Itys
scenes.summary: Progne plans revenge, is briefly softened by her son Itys, then hardens and with Philomela kills him and cooks his limbs.
scenes.stakes: Itys loses his life; Progne risks her own motherhood and the sisters' safety.

scenes.title: The horrible banquet
scenes.summary: Tereus unknowingly eats his son, asks for Itys, and Philomela throws the bloody head at him; he rages and weeps.
scenes.stakes: Tereus faces the horror of his crime's revenge; the sisters face his sword.

scenes.title: Transformed into birds
scenes.summary: The sisters become a swallow and a nightingale, and Tereus a crested lapwing; Pandion dies of grief.
scenes.stakes: The sisters escape death only by flight; Tereus is condemned to bird form.

alias_notes.explanation: A ritual cry of Bacchic worshippers, not a name of the god.
The sisters, Athenian princes, called after Cecrops, legendary Athenian king; also applies to Philomela.

notable_quotes.reason: Progne rejects tears and declares her turn to violent revenge.
Chilling line showing Progne hardening her heart against pity.

analysis.text: The episode shows vengeance escalating into horror, where cruelty is answered with greater cruelty and family bonds are destroyed.
The Bacchic rites, which let women roam at night in disguise, supply the cover for the escape; Greeks and Romans associated them with frenzy.

legacy.text: The story of Philomela as nightingale became a standard poetic image, used by later poets including Shakespeare in Titus Andronicus, which echoes the tale directly.

fun_facts.text: Ovid's Latin pun is lost here: the bird 'epops' is the hoopoe, which the translator renders as lapwing.

language_notes.text: Sithonian means Thracian, from the Sithonii, a people of Thrace. Here it marks the setting as Tereus's kingdom.
Rhodope is a mountain range in Thrace, long associated with Bacchic revels.
Progne pretends her fury is inspired by Bacchus, so her rage passes as ritual frenzy. The sentence turns to address the god directly.
"Evoë!" was the ritual cry of Bacchus's worshippers in their ecstatic rites.
"Supplanter of her sister" means Philomela feels she has displaced Progne as Tereus's partner, though she was forced. Her hand stands in for speech because her tongue was cut out.
"The members that have deprived thee of thy chastity" is a euphemism for Tereus's genitals, which Progne threatens to cut off.
"In truth" is a narrator's aside: Progne really was moved. The "mother" in her is her maternal feeling, which she now struggles against.
Pandion was king of Athens and father of Progne and Philomela. Progne is reminding herself of her own family's honour.
The Ganges stands for the far, wild East, so the tigress is an exotic, ferocious predator.
"His wife" is Progne (Procne), who serves Tereus his own son; "unconsciousness" means he is unaware of what the meal is.
The "Viperous sisters" are the Furies, snake-haired goddesses of vengeance, called up from the Stygian valley, the underworld around the river Styx.
"Thracian" names Tereus, king of Thrace, a region north of Greece.
"Cecropian" means Athenian, after Cecrops, legendary first king of Athens; the sisters are daughters of Pandion, an Athenian king.
In the usual tradition one sister becomes a nightingale of the woods and the other a swallow dwelling under house roofs; the text does not say which is which.
Tartarus is here the underworld, the realm of the dead ("shades").

context_notes.text: Bacchus is the god of wine and ecstasy. His women worshippers, Bacchantes, roamed at night in frenzy, which gave Progne a cover for her rescue.
Vine leaves, a deerskin and a light spear (the thyrsus) were the standard dress of a Bacchante.
The house is accursed because Tereus raped Philomela and imprisoned her after cutting out her tongue.
Progne is the wife of Tereus, king of Thrace. He raped her sister Philomela and cut out her tongue to silence her.
Itys is the young son of Progne and Tereus. His death becomes the vengeance on his father.
Progne and Philomela will serve the boy's cooked flesh to Tereus at a feast, a revenge that echoes the myth of Atreus and Thyestes.
The "throne of his forefathers" stresses Tereus's royal pride, which makes his unwitting cannibalism more degrading.
Philomela cannot speak because Tereus raped her and cut out her tongue to silence her; this is why she longs for words.

literary_notes.text: Night is said to be "conscious" of the rites, as if it were a witness. This lends the scene secrecy and menace.
The narrator suddenly addresses Bacchus, giving the moment a charged, almost ritual intensity.
Philomela's shudder and pallor show her terror at returning to the scene of her violation without needing to state it.
Philomela feels shame and guilt though she is the victim, and her hand replaces her silenced voice.
Itys's likeness to his father, which gives the boy his appeal, is what turns Progne against him.
Progne inverts moral terms, calling tenderness a crime, and so justifies her own cruelty to herself.
Itys is compared to a hind's fawn dragged by a tigress, stressing his helplessness and the predatory cruelty of his own mother.
The boy's cries of "Alas!" and "My mother!" as he clings to his killer heighten the horror, and the unturned face shows her resolve.
The father who sits proudly aloft devours his own flesh, a grim reversal of his royal dignity.
Tereus asks for the son he has just eaten, while the reader and the women know the truth.
The line repeats itself, affirming the wonder: the supposed impression turns out to be literal fact, which makes the transformation abrupt.
Blood-stained feathers and breast mark the birds permanently with the crime, linking the metamorphosis to guilt and vengeance.
The sword-like "long spear" becomes a bill, showing his violent nature preserved in his new bodily form.
